segments.narration: A three-ton stone lion flew over Beijing's city wall. The thirtieth of May, 1626, mid-morning, in the reign of the Tianqi Emperor.
Everything inside two kilometres was gone. The ground at the centre dropped six metres, and full-grown trees came down out at Miyun, far outside the city.
Witnesses described a coloured cloud shaped like a black mushroom, hanging there for hours. What flattens a capital city in 1626?
The centre of it was the Wanggongchang armoury, one of six imperial gunpowder works, normally staffed by eighty people. As many as twenty thousand died.
Gunpowder is the obvious answer and still an unproven one. Historians have floated a meteor airburst too. The emperor's seven-month-old heir died after it.

verdicts.claim: On 30 May 1626 an explosion in Beijing threw a stone lion of about three tonnes over the city wall.
verdicts.note: 75% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Everything within about 2 km was destroyed across roughly 4 square kilometres, the ground at the epicentre sank about 6.5 m, and large trees were thrown as far as Miyun.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Witnesses described a multicoloured, silk-like cloud compared to a black lingzhi mushroom that lingered over the site for hours.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records the silk-like, multicoloured, black-lingzhi-mushroom descriptions lingering for hours; The World of Chinese notes the mushroom-shaped cloud reports and that they have fed conspiracy theories.

verdicts.claim: The blast was centred on the Wanggongchang Armoury, one of six Ministry of Works gunpowder factories near Beijing, normally staffed by 70 to 80 people, and the death toll is put as high as 20,000.
verdicts.note: 79% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: There is no academic consensus on the cause; a gunpowder explosion is most commonly suspected, with a meteor airburst and a natural gas explosion also proposed, and the Tianqi Emperor's seven-month-old heir Zhu Cijiong died after the event.
